title: Weldon's lace stole
subtitle: A rectangular fingering stole in a Victorian vine-and-leaf lace pattern from Weldon's series.
excerpt: A rectangular stole in fingering-weight wool, worked lengthwise in a vine-and-leaf lace pattern reproduced from Weldon's Practical Knitter, 7th series (1892). Finished size approximately 45 cm wide by 180 cm long, blocked. About 300 g of fingering yarn. Cast on lengthwise at the full width.

glossaryTerms.definition: A lace pattern in which yarn-over increases paired with matched decreases create a diagonal vine motif across the fabric. Each vine repeat produces a slight bias to the fabric that is corrected by blocking.

content.text: A rectangular stole in fingering-weight wool worked lengthwise in the
vine lace
pattern from Weldon's Practical Knitter. Finished size approximately 45 × 180 cm.

The vine lace is an 8-stitch 10-row repeat with a natural diagonal bias; blocking corrects this fully. Working lengthwise means the cast-on carries the width and the rows carry the length, so the 864-stitch cast-on is worked once and the piece grows across 864 rows to the 180 cm length. Budget about 300 g (about 1,200 m / 1,310 yards) of fingering wool.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: About 300 g (1,200 m / 1,310 yards) of fingering-weight yarn

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 3.75 mm (UK 9 / US 5) circular needle, 120 cm or longer

items.name: Stitch markers
items.qty: Several to mark lace repeat boundaries

items.name: Tapestry needle, scissors, blocking mat, pins

content.text: Gauge

24 stitches and 48 rows to 10 cm over stockinette on 3.75 mm needles, blocked. The vine lace pattern runs slightly taller than stockinette: 40 rows to 10 cm in the pattern stitch (rather than 48 rows), because the yarn-overs create more open structure per row. At pattern stitch gauge, the 180 cm long stole requires approximately 720 rows. Plan for approximately 720 to 750 pattern rows total.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast on

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 108 stitches (4 sts border + 100 sts body in 12.5 × 8-stitch repeats + 4 sts border). For the long-tail, allow a tail of approximately (3.75 × 108) / 10 + 15 = 55.5 cm.
Vine lace repeat (8 sts, 10 rows)

Work a 4-stitch garter border on each short end throughout. Body stitches (100): RS Row 1: *k1, yo, k2, ssk, k2tog, k2, yo; repeat from *. RS Row 3: *k2, yo, k1, ssk, k2tog, k1, yo, k1; repeat from *. RS Row 5: *k3, yo, ssk, k2tog, yo, k1, yo; repeat from *. RS Row 7: *k1, k2tog, k2, yo, k1, yo, k2, ssk; repeat from *. RS Row 9: k1, k2tog, k1, yo, k3, yo, k1, ssk. WS rows (2, 4, 6, 8, 10): p across body, k4 border each side.
Continue the 10-row repeat until the length reaches 180 cm, then work 6 garter rows before binding off.
Bind off
Work Jeny's surprisingly stretchy bind-off. The cast-on end has a natural long-tail edge; the bind-off end must match it in elasticity.
Stitch count check-ins
Every 10 rows (one complete repeat): stitch count must remain 108. Any deviation means a yarn-over was missed or an extra k2tog was worked. If you find a mismatch, tink back to the last lifeline.
Common faults
Diagonal bias before blocking is normal. The vine motif is diagonal by design; it straightens fully with firm pinning.

Stitch count fluctuating: one of the two decreases (ssk or k2tog) was omitted on a RS row. The vine repeat balances exactly: each row must have one yo, one ssk, and one k2tog. Count these three elements on every RS row.
Blocking

Soak in cool water 20 minutes, press out in towels. Pin both short ends to 45 cm. Pin both long edges to 180 cm. Use generous pins to correct any remaining diagonal bias. The vine motif should be clearly visible after blocking.
Care
Hand wash in cool water, lay flat to dry. Re-block every few wears to maintain the lace openness and straight edges.
What to try next
Work the same stole in lace-weight yarn on 3.25 mm needles at the same cast-on count for a finer, more translucent stole approximately 36 × 150 cm.
